lead: Horizontal and vertical angles are the two numbers a theodolite exists to produce. A horizontal angle is the turn between two sight lines projected on a horizontal plane. It fixes direction in a traverse, a triangulation net or a building layout. A vertical angle is the rise or fall of a sight line above or below the horizontal; with a distance it gives a height. The instrument reads a graduated circle through verniers. Both faces are observed and averaged, so instrument errors cancel instead of entering the answer.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for the axes, clamps, tangent screws and the meaning of face left and face right.

sections.h3: Horizontal angle by the ordinary method

blocks.text: A horizontal angle at station O between targets A and B is the angle between the vertical planes O-A and O-B. It is measured in the horizontal plane. The horizontal circle is graduated clockwise in degrees. Two verniers, A and B, sit 180° apart. Reading both and averaging removes eccentricity of the centres.

items: Set up the theodolite over O, level it, focus the telescope and eyepiece. Work face left.
Clamp the lower plate. Release the upper clamp, turn to A, bisect, and clamp the upper clamp. Set the circle near zero with the upper tangent screw.

Read both verniers. For each vernier, read the degrees on the main scale at the mark just before that vernier's zero, and read minutes and seconds from the vernier divisions. Do this for A and for B separately. Then reduce B by 180° and average it with A.
Release the upper clamp, turn clockwise to B, bisect, and read both verniers. Angle AOB = mean reading at B − mean reading at A. If A was set to zero, it is the mean reading at B.

Transit the telescope, set face right, and repeat. The mean of the face-left and face-right angles is the result. The mean of the faces is free of collimation error. Half the difference between the face-left and face-right angles is the error collimation caused in this angle, about c(sec h₂ − sec h₁), where c is the instrument's collimation error and h₁, h₂ are the altitudes of the two sights; it measures the instrument's collimation error only when the two sights are steep and differ in altitude.

blocks.where: θ is the mean horizontal reading in degrees; A and B are the two vernier readings in degrees. Use +180° when B is less than 180°, and −180° when B is greater.

blocks.text: Repetition turns the same angle n times on the circle without resetting. Each turn uses a different part of the graduation, so a graduation error at one place tends to cancel. The final reading divided by n gives the angle.

items: Set zero on A as before. Turn to B and read R1.
Clamp the upper plate to the lower plate. Release the lower clamp, turn the whole instrument back to A. The reading does not change.
Clamp the lower plate. Release the upper clamp, turn to B again. The reading is now R2 = 2θ. Repeat n times to get Rn.
Compute θ = (Rn − R0)/n. R0 is the starting reading; if R0 = 0, θ = Rn/n.

blocks.where: θ is the required angle; Rn is the final reading after n repetitions; R0 is the initial reading; n is the number of repetitions.

blocks.text: The direction method, also called reiteration, is used when several directions are observed from one station. Set zero on a reference direction. Observe each direction in clockwise order on both faces. Close the horizon by sighting the reference again. The final reading should be 360° from the start. Any difference e is the closing error. Apply the correction −e/m cumulatively to the observed directions, starting with 0 at the reference and adding −e/m at each step, so the closing sight of the reference gets −e. Do not subtract a flat −e/m from every direction.
correction at k-th direction = −k e / m
blocks.where: e is the closing error in seconds, final reading minus 360°; m is the number of observed directions including the reference; k is the direction count from the first reference. k = 0 at the reference, k = 1 at the next observed direction, and k = m at the closing sight of the reference. The correction at k = m is −e.

sections.h3: Vertical angles and the errors that remain

blocks.text: A vertical angle is measured in a vertical plane. It is the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal (altitude), or between the line of sight and the zenith (zenith distance). Elevation is above the horizontal and positive. Depression is below and negative.

The vertical circle is fixed to the telescope. Its zero may be at the horizon or at the zenith. On an altitude graduation, 0° is horizontal and 90° is zenith. On a zenith-distance graduation, 0° is zenith and 90° is horizontal. To find the graduation of the vertical circle, sight a nearly horizontal object on face left. If it reads about 0° the circle is graduated as altitude; if it reads about 90° it is graduated as zenith distance.

blocks.where: α is altitude, positive above the horizon and negative below; z is zenith distance in degrees. z = 90 gives α = 0; z = 0 gives α = +90°; z = 120° gives α = −30°.

blocks.text: Sight the target on face left and read the vertical circle. Transit, set face right, sight the same target, and read again. Reduce each reading to the same quadrant. The mean is α = ½(α_L + α_R). The half difference is the index error. A depression must carry a minus sign; a zenith reading above 90° already tells you it is a depression. A vertical angle with a horizontal distance gives a height; see Chapter 4.3.
Most angle errors are removed by both faces. The common ones are:

items: Eccentricity of centres: the centre of the graduated horizontal circle does not coincide with the vertical axis about which the instrument turns, so each vernier reads a slightly wrong angle. Reading both verniers, which sit 180° apart, and averaging removes it.
Collimation: the line of sight is not perpendicular to the horizontal axis. The mean of faces removes it.

Vertical axis not truly vertical: the whole circle is tilted, so angles between steep sights are wrong and the error does not reverse when the telescope is transited. The mean of faces does not remove it. Level the instrument carefully, check the plate and altitude bubbles, and keep sights short and near the horizontal.
Graduation error: circle divisions are imperfect. Repetition and changing circle positions reduce it.
Bisection and refraction: a blurred target or a sight close to hot ground bends the line. Use short sights, set targets high, avoid midday shimmer.
Index error of the vertical circle: zero is off the true horizon or zenith. The mean of faces removes it.

examples.question: A horizontal angle AOB is measured by the repetition method with a 20″ theodolite, starting from a zero reading. After 4 repetitions the vernier reads 148°24′40″. Face left gives 37°06′20″ and face right gives 37°06′00″. Find the angle by repetition, the mean of faces, and the half difference.
steps: Divide by the number of repetitions: θ = 534280″ / 4 = 133570″ = 37°06′10″.
Convert face readings: face left = 37°06′20″ = 133580″; face right = 37°06′00″ = 133560″.

Half difference = (133580″ − 133560″) / 2 = 10″. This is the error collimation caused in this particular angle; it measures the instrument's collimation error only when the two sights are steep and differ in altitude.
examples.answer: Angle AOB = 37°06′10″ (133570″); the face mean is also 37°06′10″, and the half difference is 10″, the collimation effect in this angle.
examples.check:
def s(d,m,t): return d*3600+m*60+t
R=s(148,24,40); n=4; a=R/n
L=s(37,6,20); F=s(37,6,0); m=(L+F)/2; h=(L-F)/2
print(a); print(L); print(F); print(m); print(h)

traps: Face right read at face value: the face-right reading of a direction is about 180° from its face-left reading. Reduce the face-right mean reading by 180° (add 180° if it is less than 180°) and only then average it with the face-left value. Reducing vernier B by 180° is a separate rule, used within each face.
A depression entered as positive: the sign carries into trigonometric levelling and reverses the height.
Using a zenith distance as an altitude: α = 90° − z, not z itself.
Forgetting R0 in repetition: θ = (Rn − R0)/n, not Rn/n, when the start is not zero.
Averaging A and B without the 180° correction: the mean is meaningless.

quiz.a: The angle between two vertical planes through the station and the two targets, measured in the horizontal plane.

quiz.q: Why are verniers A and B both read and averaged?
quiz.a: They sit 180° apart. Their mean removes the error from eccentricity of the centres, after reducing B by 180°.

quiz.q: A horizontal angle gives face left 42°18′20″ and face right 42°17′40″. Find the mean and the half difference.
Why does the repetition method reduce graduation error?
quiz.a: Each repetition reads a different part of the circle. A periodic graduation error at one position tends to cancel over n turns, and the total is divided by n.

quiz.q: A zenith distance is 103°12′. Find the altitude.
quiz.a: α = 90° − 103°12′ = −13°12′, so it is a depression of 13°12′.

quiz.q: Four directions are observed and the horizon closes with a closing error of +24″. State the cumulative corrections.
quiz.a: e = +24″, m = 4, so −e/m = −6″. Apply cumulatively: 0 at the reference, then −6″, −12″, −18″ at the next directions, and −24″ at the closing sight of the reference. The horizon then closes exactly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Total stations and digital theodolites read angles electronically and apply dual-axis compensator corrections, but the face-left/face-right check still catches collimation and index errors. Search for 'zenith distance vs altitude', 'repetition method theodolite', 'closing the horizon direction method' and 'dual-axis compensator'.
